paragraphs.text: Parkinson disease-8 (PARK8) is an autosomal dominant form of parkinsonism. Clinically it closely resembles idiopathic Parkinson disease (PD), with bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and impaired postural reflexes that respond to levodopa, and a slowly progressive course (Wszolek et al., 1995). The neuropathology varies, even within a single family, and includes brainstem dopaminergic degeneration with Lewy body PD, diffuse Lewy body disease, nigral degeneration without distinctive histopathology, and progressive supranuclear palsy-like pathology (Zimprich et al., 2004). Penetrance is incomplete (Funayama et al., 2002).

paragraphs.text: Wszolek et al. (1995) described family D, a western Nebraska kindred whose ancestors probably came from England. The pedigree contained 188 individuals spanning 6 generations, 18 of whom were affected, and inheritance was autosomal dominant. Affected members developed typical levodopa-responsive PD with bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and impaired postural reflexes, and the disease progressed slowly. Eye movement abnormalities, pyramidal and cerebellar signs, sensory disturbances, and orthostatic blood pressure changes did not occur. In 1 affected individual, [18F]-6-fluoro-L-dopa PET showed decreased uptake in a pattern consistent with PD. Autopsy of another affected individual showed neuronal and pigmentary loss, gliosis, and Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The authors concluded that the disorder closely resembled, if it was not identical to, idiopathic PD.

paragraphs.text: Marras et al. (2011) compared 25 individuals with LRRK2 G2019S-associated PD with 84 individuals with idiopathic PD. Tremor was more often a presenting feature in the LRRK2 group. LRRK2-PD patients also had better olfactory identification, higher Beck Depression Inventory scores, and higher error scores on the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test of color discrimination, although overall the phenotype largely overlapped with idiopathic PD. Postural or action tremor was more common among 29 nonmanifesting G2019S carriers than among 53 noncarrier family members, suggesting that it may be an early sign. Nonparkinsonian family members had higher UPDRS motor scores, more constipation, and worse color discrimination than controls, whether or not they carried the mutation.
